title: Practicing Continuous Integration and Deployment
summary: "Automation" sounds grand — familiar to backend folks, a bit distant for frontend. Here's how I've been practicing it on frontend projects.
markdown:
## Intro

"Automation" sounds sacred and a little high-end. Backend developers usually live with it; for frontend it can still feel far away. Below is how I've practiced automation on frontend projects.

## Approaches

- One path I use a lot at work: Docker + Jenkins. Jenkins is the classic continuous-integration tool.
- The other: DaoCloud

What is continuous integration?

Jenkins has a fairly high setup cost — you need a full Jenkins environment — but it's heavily used. I'll focus on the second option: lower cost, still enough to automate the flow.

## Concrete steps

This is the automated build process for my blog.

1. Add a `Dockerfile` at the project root. That turns the manual commands into a script the system can run for you. A Dockerfile is the essential config for containerizing a project.

![image]()

1. Automated image builds (via GitHub). The code source points at your repo; once linked, actions on that source can trigger continuous integration and image builds. Pick the target project, name the image, create it. Open the pipeline definition, run a manual build against the branch you want. When that succeeds, automated build is working.

1. Deploy the built image to your own host. Hit deploy latest on the target project — when that succeeds, use the link they show to open the deployed app. Turn on auto-publish so every push to the target branch rebuilds and redeploys.
